Study guide · Autumn 2018 · Andrew Ng

Locally Weighted & Logistic Regression

Lecture 3 covers four things in seventy-five minutes: a non-parametric regression algorithm, a probabilistic justification for least squares, the first classification algorithm, and a second-order optimizer. This guide reconstructs all four at full derivation detail — every algebraic step written out — and then fills in the fourteen places where the lecture asserts something, defers it, or quietly skips it.

00 · Orientation

The 60-second map

Four topics, and one idea that ties three of them together. Read this before anything else; come back to it when a derivation stops making sense.

The lecture looks like four unrelated things. It isn't. Topics 2, 3 and 4 are one continuous argument, and topic 1 is a self-contained detour that Ng puts first because it answers a question students ask at the end of Lecture 2 ("how do I choose features?").

The one sentence to remember

Almost every algorithm in this lecture comes from the same recipe: assume a distribution for yyy given xxx, write the likelihood of the training data, take logs, and climb. Least squares comes from a Gaussian; logistic regression comes from a Bernoulli. Newton's method is just a faster way to climb.

01 · Topic 1

Locally weighted regression

The algorithm that lets you stop agonising over which features to use — as long as you have few inputs and lots of data.

The problem it solves

Lecture 2 left you with a question. To fit house prices you wrote hθ(x)=θ0+θ1xh_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1 xhθ​(x)=θ0​+θ1​x. But what if the relationship curves? You could add x2x^2x2; you could add x\sqrt{x}x​; you could add log⁡x\log xlogx. Each choice is a guess, and a bad guess underfits (the model can't represent the truth) or overfits (the model chases noise). Ng's framing:

  • Underfitting — the model has too little capacity to capture structure that is really there. A straight line through a clearly curved cloud.
  • Overfitting — the model has so much capacity that it fits the sampling noise as well as the signal. A degree-5 polynomial through six points passes through all six and predicts nonsense between them.
Gap 1 · Ng draws this picture but never defines the axis

The lecture shows underfit/overfit as a picture and moves on. The quantity being traded off has a name and a decomposition worth knowing now, because it explains every hyperparameter you will ever tune. For a fixed test point, the expected squared error of a learned predictor f^\hat ff^​ splits into three pieces:

E[(y−f^(x))2]  =  (E[f^(x)]−f(x))2⏟bias2  +  Var⁡ ⁣(f^(x))⏟variance  +  σ2⏟irreducible\mathbb{E}\big[(y-\hat f(x))^2\big] \;=\; \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)]-f(x)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} \;+\; \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\!\big(\hat f(x)\big)}_{\text{variance}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}}E[(y−f^​(x))2]=bias2(E[f^​(x)]−f(x))2​​+varianceVar(f^​(x))​​+irreducibleσ2​​

Underfitting is bias-dominated; overfitting is variance-dominated; the third term is the noise floor no model can beat. Every knob in this lecture — the bandwidth τ\tauτ, the regularisation strength λ\lambdaλ — moves you along this trade-off. CS229 treats it formally in the bias–variance lecture; knowing the shape now makes topic 1 make sense.

Parametric versus non-parametric

This distinction is the conceptual payload of topic 1, and Ng's definition is precise and worth memorising verbatim:

Definition

A parametric learning algorithm fits a fixed, finite set of parameters θ\thetaθ to the data, and then throws the data away. Prediction cost does not depend on mmm.

A non-parametric learning algorithm needs to keep the training set around in order to make predictions. The amount of stuff you must retain grows (typically linearly) with mmm.

"Non-parametric" does not mean "no parameters". Locally weighted regression has parameters — it has a fresh θ\thetaθ for every query point. What it lacks is a fixed parameter vector that summarises the training set.

The algorithm

Put the two algorithms side by side. This is the whole idea:

Ordinary linear regressionLocally weighted regression
FitOnce, ahead of time: choose θ\thetaθ to minimise ∑i(y(i)−θTx(i))2\displaystyle\sum_i \big(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\big)^2i∑​(y(i)−θTx(i))2Once per query point xxx: choose θ\thetaθ to minimise ∑iw(i)(y(i)−θTx(i))2\displaystyle\sum_i w^{(i)}\big(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\big)^2i∑​w(i)(y(i)−θTx(i))2
PredictOutput θTx\theta^TxθTxOutput θTx\theta^TxθTx (with that query's own θ\thetaθ)
WeightsAll examples count equallyw(i)=exp⁡(−(x(i)−x)22τ2)w^{(i)}=\exp\left(-\dfrac{\left(x^{(i)}-x\right)^2}{2\tau^2}\right)w(i)=exp(−2τ2(x(i)−x)2​)
Keeps data?NoYes — all of it, forever

Read the weight formula slowly, because it is doing something simple. If x(i)x^{(i)}x(i) is close to the query point xxx, then (x(i)−x)2≈0(x^{(i)}-x)^2 \approx 0(x(i)−x)2≈0, so w(i)≈exp⁡(0)=1w^{(i)}\approx \exp(0)=1w(i)≈exp(0)=1: that example counts fully. If x(i)x^{(i)}x(i) is far away, (x(i)−x)2(x^{(i)}-x)^2(x(i)−x)2 is large, so w(i)≈exp⁡(−large)≈0w^{(i)}\approx \exp(-\text{large})\approx 0w(i)≈exp(−large)≈0: that example is effectively deleted from the training set for this one prediction.

For vector-valued inputs the numerator becomes a squared Euclidean distance, (x(i)−x)T(x(i)−x)\left(x^{(i)}-x\right)^T\left(x^{(i)}-x\right)(x(i)−x)T(x(i)−x), and in the fully general form a positive-definite matrix Σ\SigmaΣ can shape the neighbourhood: w(i)=exp⁡ ⁣(−12(x(i)−x)TΣ−1(x(i)−x))w^{(i)}=\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 (x^{(i)}-x)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x^{(i)}-x)\right)w(i)=exp(−21​(x(i)−x)TΣ−1(x(i)−x)).

Trap · the bell curve is not a probability

The weighting function looks exactly like a Gaussian density, and it is not one. There is no normalising constant 1/2πτ1/\sqrt{2\pi}\tau1/2π​τ, nothing integrates to 1, and τ\tauτ is not a standard deviation of anything random. It is a bump-shaped function chosen because it is smooth, positive and decays. Ng flags this in passing; students conflate it with the Gaussian in topic 2 constantly. They are unrelated uses of the same shape.

Solving the weighted problem — every step

Ng writes the weighted cost and says the closed form is "an exercise". Here it is in full. Let W=diag⁡(w(1),…,w(m))W=\operatorname{diag}(w^{(1)},\dots,w^{(m)})W=diag(w(1),…,w(m)), an m×mm\times mm×m diagonal matrix of weights, and let XXX and yyy be the usual design matrix and target vector.

Derivation 1 · the weighted normal equation
  1. Write the cost in matrix form.
    JW(θ)=∑i=1mw(i)(y(i)−θTx(i))2=(y−Xθ)TW(y−Xθ)J_W(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^m w^{(i)}\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2=(y-X\theta)^T W (y-X\theta)JW​(θ)=i=1∑m​w(i)(y(i)−θTx(i))2=(y−Xθ)TW(y−Xθ)
    Why this works: the vector y−Xθy-X\thetay−Xθ has iii-th entry y(i)−θTx(i)y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}y(i)−θTx(i); sandwiching a diagonal matrix multiplies the iii-th squared entry by w(i)w^{(i)}w(i) before summing.
  2. Expand the quadratic form.
    JW(θ)=yTWy−yTWXθ−θTXTWy+θTXTWXθJ_W(\theta)=y^TWy-y^TWX\theta-\theta^TX^TWy+\theta^TX^TWX\thetaJW​(θ)=yTWy−yTWXθ−θTXTWy+θTXTWXθ
    The two middle terms are scalars and are transposes of each other, and WT=WW^T=WWT=W because WWW is diagonal — so they are equal, and we may write −2θTXTWy-2\theta^TX^TWy−2θTXTWy.
  3. Differentiate with respect to θ\thetaθ.
    ∇θJW=−2XTWy+2XTWXθ\nabla_\theta J_W = -2X^TWy + 2X^TWX\theta∇θ​JW​=−2XTWy+2XTWXθ
    Uses two standard identities: ∇θ(θTa)=a\nabla_\theta(\theta^Ta)=a∇θ​(θTa)=a and ∇θ(θTAθ)=2Aθ\nabla_\theta(\theta^TA\theta)=2A\theta∇θ​(θTAθ)=2Aθ for symmetric AAA (and XTWXX^TWXXTWX is symmetric).
  4. Set the gradient to zero and solve.
    XTWX θ=XTWy⟹  θ=(XTWX)−1XTWy  X^TWX\,\theta = X^TWy \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\theta = (X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWy\;}XTWXθ=XTWy⟹θ=(XTWX)−1XTWy​
    Setting a gradient to zero finds a stationary point; because JWJ_WJW​ is a convex quadratic in θ\thetaθ (the Hessian 2XTWX2X^TWX2XTWX is positive semidefinite whenever all w(i)≥0w^{(i)}\ge 0w(i)≥0), that stationary point is a global minimum.
  5. Sanity check. Put W=IW=IW=I (every weight equal to 1) and you recover the ordinary normal equation θ=(XTX)−1XTy\theta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Tyθ=(XTX)−1XTy from Lecture 2.

In code this is four lines, and it runs once per prediction:

def lwr_predict(x_query, X, y, tau):
    w   = np.exp(-((X[:,1] - x_query)**2) / (2*tau**2))   # m weights
    A   = X.T @ (w[:,None] * X)          # X^T W X, without building the m x m matrix
    b   = X.T @ (w * y)                  # X^T W y
    th  = np.linalg.solve(A + 1e-8*np.eye(X.shape[1]), b)  # never use inv()
    return np.array([1.0, x_query]) @ th

Two implementation notes that matter and that the lecture does not give you. First, never materialise the m×mm\times mm×m matrix WWW — broadcasting w[:,None] * X costs O(mn)O(mn)O(mn) instead of O(m2)O(m^2)O(m2). Second, the small ridge term 1e-8*I is not decoration: when τ\tauτ is small, almost every weight underflows to zero and XTWXX^TWXXTWX becomes numerically singular.

What τ\tauτ does

The bandwidth τ\tauτ is the only hyperparameter, and it controls exactly the bias–variance trade-off from Fig. 1 — but continuously rather than in integer steps of polynomial degree.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 2 · how you actually choose τ

Ng says "there is a way to choose τ\tauτ" and moves on. The way is hold-out validation or k-fold cross-validation: split off data the fit never sees, sweep τ\tauτ over a log-spaced grid, and take the minimiser of held-out error. Training error is useless here — it decreases monotonically as τ→0\tau\to 0τ→0, because with a tiny bandwidth every prediction is essentially reading the answer off the nearest training point.

Gap 3 · the four practical facts that decide whether you can use this at all

(a) Cost per prediction. Every single prediction touches all mmm training points and solves an (n+1)×(n+1)(n{+}1)\times(n{+}1)(n+1)×(n+1) system: O(mn+mn2+n3)O(mn + mn^2 + n^3)O(mn+mn2+n3) per query. Ordinary linear regression costs O(n)O(n)O(n) per query after training. For mmm in the millions this is the difference between a service that responds and one that doesn't. Ng mentions kd-trees as a fix — the idea is to index the training points spatially so you can ignore the ones whose weights would be negligible.

(b) The curse of dimensionality. The method assumes there are neighbours near the query point. In high dimensions there are not. To capture a fraction ppp of uniformly distributed data in ddd dimensions you need a hypercube of edge length p1/dp^{1/d}p1/d — in 10 dimensions, capturing 10% of your points requires stretching 80% of the way along every single axis. Your "local" neighbourhood is the whole dataset. This is why Ng restricts the recommendation to low-dimensional problems.

(c) Feature scaling is mandatory. The weights depend on Euclidean distance, so a feature measured in dollars and a feature measured in bedrooms are not comparable. Standardise every feature to zero mean and unit variance before computing weights, or one feature silently dominates the neighbourhood. The lecture never mentions this and it will break your first implementation on real data.

(d) It is memory, not a model. Shipping a locally weighted regressor means shipping the training set. That has licensing, privacy and storage consequences that a parametric model does not have.

Gap 4 · three refinements that are standard practice and absent from the lecture

A compactly supported kernel. The Gaussian kernel never assigns exactly zero weight, so every prediction genuinely uses all mmm points. Cleveland's LOESS uses the tricube kernel w(u)=(1−∣u∣3)3w(u)=(1-|u|^3)^3w(u)=(1−∣u∣3)3 for ∣u∣<1|u|<1∣u∣<1 and 000 otherwise, where uuu is distance scaled by the span. Points outside the span get weight exactly zero — sparse, cheaper, and it makes the kd-tree trick actually pay off.

Local linear, not local constant. Fitting a weighted constant instead of a weighted line gives the Nadaraya–Watson kernel estimator, which has a well-known bias problem at the edges of the data (near the boundary all the neighbours are on one side, so a constant is pulled toward the interior). Fitting a local line automatically corrects this to first order. Ng's choice of a line rather than a constant is not arbitrary, and this is the reason.

Robustness iterations. LOWESS runs the fit, computes residuals, downweights points with large residuals via a bisquare function, and refits — typically three times. This makes the smoother resistant to outliers, which plain locally weighted least squares is not.

Gap 5 · the idea generalises past regression

Nothing about local weighting is specific to squared error. Locally weighted logistic regression is a real algorithm: at each query point, maximise ∑iw(i)[y(i)log⁡h+(1−y(i))log⁡(1−h)]\sum_i w^{(i)}\left[y^{(i)}\log h + (1-y^{(i)})\log(1-h)\right]∑i​w(i)[y(i)logh+(1−y(i))log(1−h)] instead. It appears on CS229 problem sets. Once you have finished topic 3 of this lecture, come back and write down its gradient — it is a two-line change.

02 · Topic 2

Why squared error? The probabilistic interpretation

Nobody chose 12∑(h−y)2\frac12\sum(h-y)^221​∑(h−y)2 because it looked nice. Under one assumption about noise, it is forced on you.

Ng opens this topic by admitting the awkwardness: in Lecture 2 the squared-error cost was pulled out of thin air. Why squared and not absolute value, or fourth power? The answer is that a set of probabilistic assumptions makes least squares the maximum-likelihood estimate, and those assumptions are ones people are often willing to make.

The assumptions, stated precisely

Model

y(i)=θTx(i)+ε(i),ε(i) ∼i.i.d. N(0,σ2)y^{(i)}=\theta^Tx^{(i)}+\varepsilon^{(i)},\qquad \varepsilon^{(i)}\ \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\ \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)y(i)=θTx(i)+ε(i),ε(i) ∼i.i.d. N(0,σ2)

There is a true θ\thetaθ. Each observed target equals the linear prediction plus an error term. The error terms are independent and identically distributed Gaussians with mean zero.

Ng's justification for the Gaussian is deliberately loose, and he says so: the error absorbs many small unmodelled effects, and sums of many independent small effects tend toward a Gaussian by the central limit theorem. It is a modelling choice, not a fact about the world.

Because ε(i)=y(i)−θTx(i)\varepsilon^{(i)}=y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}ε(i)=y(i)−θTx(i), the density of the error becomes a density for yyy given xxx:

p ⁣(ε(i))=12π σexp⁡ ⁣(−(ε(i))22σ2)⟹p ⁣(y(i)∣x(i);θ)=12π σexp⁡ ⁣(−(y(i)−θTx(i))22σ2)p\!\left(\varepsilon^{(i)}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(\varepsilon^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)p(ε(i))=2π​σ1​exp(−2σ2(ε(i))2​)⟹p(y(i)∣x(i);θ)=2π​σ1​exp(−2σ2(y(i)−θTx(i))2​)
Trap · the semicolon

Ng is emphatic about p(y(i)∣x(i);θ)p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta)p(y(i)∣x(i);θ) rather than p(y(i)∣x(i),θ)p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)},\theta)p(y(i)∣x(i),θ). The comma would say θ\thetaθ is a random variable we are conditioning on; the semicolon says θ\thetaθ is a fixed but unknown parameter that the density depends on. This is the frequentist stance, and it is what makes the phrase "maximum likelihood" meaningful. When you switch to a Bayesian view in Gap 8 below, the semicolon becomes a comma and the whole story changes.

From likelihood to least squares — every step

Derivation 2 · least squares is the MLE
  1. Define the likelihood as a function of the parameters, with the data held fixed.
    L(θ)=p(y⃗∣X;θ)=∏i=1mp ⁣(y(i)∣x(i);θ)L(\theta)=p(\vec{y}\mid X;\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}p\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\right)L(θ)=p(y​∣X;θ)=i=1∏m​p(y(i)∣x(i);θ)
    The product is legitimate only because of the independence assumption. This is where i.i.d. earns its keep.
  2. Substitute the Gaussian density.
    L(θ)=∏i=1m12π σexp⁡ ⁣(−(y(i)−θTx(i))22σ2)L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)L(θ)=i=1∏m​2π​σ1​exp(−2σ2(y(i)−θTx(i))2​)
  3. Take logarithms. Maximising LLL and maximising log⁡L\log LlogL give the same θ\thetaθ, because log⁡\loglog is strictly increasing.
    ℓ(θ)=log⁡L(θ)=∑i=1mlog⁡ ⁣[12π σexp⁡ ⁣(−(y(i)−θTx(i))22σ2)]\ell(\theta)=\log L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\!\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\right]ℓ(θ)=logL(θ)=i=1∑m​log[2π​σ1​exp(−2σ2(y(i)−θTx(i))2​)]
    This is the single most useful move in the lecture: log⁡\loglog turns the product into a sum, and cancels the exponential.
  4. Split the log of the product inside each term, using log⁡(ab)=log⁡a+log⁡b\log(ab)=\log a+\log blog(ab)=loga+logb and log⁡eu=u\log e^{u}=ulogeu=u.
    ℓ(θ)=∑i=1m[log⁡12π σ−(y(i)−θTx(i))22σ2]\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}-\frac{\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]ℓ(θ)=i=1∑m​[log2π​σ1​−2σ2(y(i)−θTx(i))2​]
  5. Pull the constant out of the sum.
    ℓ(θ)=mlog⁡12π σ  −  1σ2⋅12∑i=1m(y(i)−θTx(i))2\ell(\theta)=m\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\;-\;\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2ℓ(θ)=mlog2π​σ1​−σ21​⋅21​i=1∑m​(y(i)−θTx(i))2
  6. Identify what depends on θ\thetaθ. The first term does not. The factor 1/σ21/\sigma^21/σ2 is a positive constant that scales the second term but cannot move its maximiser.
    arg⁡max⁡θ ℓ(θ)  =  arg⁡min⁡θ 12∑i=1m(y(i)−θTx(i))2  =  arg⁡min⁡θ J(θ)\arg\max_\theta\ \ell(\theta)\;=\;\arg\min_\theta\ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2\;=\;\arg\min_\theta\ J(\theta)argθmax​ ℓ(θ)=argθmin​ 21​i=1∑m​(y(i)−θTx(i))2=argθmin​ J(θ)
    Maximising a negative quantity means minimising its magnitude — hence the flip from max to min.
The result

Under i.i.d. zero-mean Gaussian noise, minimising squared error is maximum likelihood estimation. The 12\frac1221​ that looked like a convenience turns out to be the 12σ2\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}2σ21​ from the Gaussian with σ\sigmaσ divided out. And the choice of σ2\sigma^2σ2 has no effect whatsoever on θ^\hat\thetaθ^ — which is why Lecture 2 could get away with never mentioning noise at all.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 6 · σ² does not vanish, it just does not affect θ

Ng notes that σ2\sigma^2σ2 "doesn't matter" and moves on, which invites the wrong conclusion that the model has nothing to say about noise. It does. Maximise ℓ\ellℓ over σ2\sigma^2σ2 as well: differentiate step 5's expression with respect to σ\sigmaσ, set to zero, and you get

σ^2=1m∑i=1m(y(i)−θ^Tx(i))2\hat\sigma^2=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(y^{(i)}-\hat\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2σ^2=m1​i=1∑m​(y(i)−θ^Tx(i))2

the mean squared residual. This estimator is biased downward, because θ^\hat\thetaθ^ was itself chosen to make those residuals small; the unbiased version divides by m−n−1m-n-1m−n−1 instead of mmm. You need σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2 for anything involving uncertainty — prediction intervals, standard errors on θ\thetaθ, hypothesis tests — none of which the lecture touches.

Gap 7 · what breaks when the assumptions break
AssumptionViolated whenConsequence & fix
Gaussian noiseHeavy tails, outliersSquared error over-reacts to outliers because it grows quadratically. A Laplace noise model gives least absolute deviations; a hybrid gives the Huber loss.
IndependenceTime series, repeated measures, clustered dataThe likelihood no longer factors. θ^\hat\thetaθ^ may still be reasonable but every uncertainty estimate is wrong (usually far too confident).
Constant variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 (homoscedasticity)Noise grows with the responseThe MLE becomes weighted least squares with w(i)=1/σi2w^{(i)}=1/\sigma_i^2w(i)=1/σi2​ — the same algebra as topic 1, arrived at for a completely different reason. See problem 8.
Zero meanSystematic bias in measurementAbsorbed into the intercept θ0\theta_0θ0​, so harmless — provided you kept x0=1x_0=1x0​=1.
Gap 8 · one line further gets you ridge regression

The lecture stops at maximum likelihood. Take one more step — treat θ\thetaθ as random with a prior θ∼N(0,τ2I)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2 I)θ∼N(0,τ2I) — and maximise the posterior instead (MAP estimation):

θ^MAP=arg⁡max⁡θ p(θ)∏ip(y(i)∣x(i),θ)=arg⁡min⁡θ 12σ2∑i(y(i)−θTx(i))2+12τ2∥θ∥2\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_\theta\ p(\theta)\prod_i p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)},\theta) =\arg\min_\theta\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\theta\|^2θ^MAP​=argθmax​ p(θ)i∏​p(y(i)∣x(i),θ)=argθmin​ 2σ21​i∑​(y(i)−θTx(i))2+2τ21​∥θ∥2

which is exactly ridge regression with λ=σ2/τ2\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2λ=σ2/τ2. Swap the Gaussian prior for a Laplace prior and you get the LASSO. Regularisation is not a hack bolted onto the loss — it is a prior. This connection makes the regularisation you will need in topic 3 feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

Gap 9 · you do not actually need the Gaussian for least squares to be good

The lecture's argument runs Gaussian ⇒ least squares, which can leave the impression that least squares is only justified under Gaussian noise. The Gauss–Markov theorem says something stronger and assumption-lighter: if the errors merely have zero mean, constant variance, and are uncorrelated — no distributional assumption at all — then ordinary least squares is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator: the minimum-variance estimator among all unbiased estimators that are linear in yyy. Gaussianity is what you need for the maximum-likelihood story and for exact finite-sample inference, not for least squares to be sensible.

03 · Topic 3

Classification and logistic regression

The first classification algorithm in the course, derived by running the topic-2 recipe with a Bernoulli instead of a Gaussian.

Now y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1}: benign or malignant, spam or not spam. By convention y=0y=0y=0 is the negative class and y=1y=1y=1 the positive class. The labels are not a scale — nothing is "twice as malignant" — so a model that outputs −0.3-0.3−0.3 or 1.41.41.4 is outputting a number that has no meaning.

Why not just use linear regression?

Ng draws this on the board and it is worth internalising because the failure mode is not obvious. Fit a straight line to the {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1} labels and threshold at 0.50.50.5. On tidy data this appears to work. Then add one more example — correctly labelled, no error at all — far out along the axis:

Two problems, then. Squared error punishes a model for being too right, and the output is unbounded so it cannot be read as a probability. Both are fixed by squashing the output.

The hypothesis

Definition

hθ(x)=g ⁣(θTx)=11+e−θTx,g(z)=11+e−zh_\theta(x)=g\!\left(\theta^Tx\right)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^Tx}},\qquad g(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}hθ​(x)=g(θTx)=1+e−θTx1​,g(z)=1+e−z1​

ggg is the sigmoid or logistic function. It maps R\mathbb{R}R onto the open interval (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), is smooth and strictly increasing, and satisfies g(0)=12g(0)=\tfrac12g(0)=21​, g(z)→1g(z)\to1g(z)→1 as z→∞z\to\inftyz→∞, g(z)→0g(z)\to0g(z)→0 as z→−∞z\to-\inftyz→−∞.

Gap 10 · why the sigmoid and not some other squashing function

Ng says other functions mapping to [0,1][0,1][0,1] would work, that the sigmoid "arises naturally", and defers the reason to the GLM lecture. You do not have to wait. Here are three independent derivations, any one of which makes the choice non-arbitrary:

1. Assume the log-odds are linear. The odds of the positive class are p/(1−p)p/(1-p)p/(1−p). Assume their logarithm is what the linear model predicts:

log⁡p1−p=θTx  ⟹  p1−p=eθTx  ⟹  p=eθTx−peθTx  ⟹  p(1+eθTx)=eθTx\log\frac{p}{1-p}=\theta^Tx \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{p}{1-p}=e^{\theta^Tx} \;\Longrightarrow\; p=e^{\theta^Tx}-pe^{\theta^Tx} \;\Longrightarrow\; p\left(1+e^{\theta^Tx}\right)=e^{\theta^Tx}log1−pp​=θTx⟹1−pp​=eθTx⟹p=eθTx−peθTx⟹p(1+eθTx)=eθTx

⟹  p=eθTx1+eθTx=11+e−θTx=g(θTx)\Longrightarrow\; p=\frac{e^{\theta^Tx}}{1+e^{\theta^Tx}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^Tx}}=g(\theta^Tx)⟹p=1+eθTxeθTx​=1+e−θTx1​=g(θTx)

The sigmoid is not an extra assumption. It is the inverse of the log-odds, and the log-odds — the "logit" — is the natural unbounded scale on which to do linear modelling with probabilities.

2. It is the canonical link of the Bernoulli. Write the Bernoulli in exponential-family form: p(y;ϕ)=ϕy(1−ϕ)1−y=exp⁡ ⁣(ylog⁡ϕ1−ϕ+log⁡(1−ϕ))p(y;\phi)=\phi^y(1-\phi)^{1-y}=\exp\!\left(y\log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}+\log(1-\phi)\right)p(y;ϕ)=ϕy(1−ϕ)1−y=exp(ylog1−ϕϕ​+log(1−ϕ)). The natural parameter is η=log⁡ϕ1−ϕ\eta=\log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}η=log1−ϕϕ​, and inverting gives ϕ=1/(1+e−η)\phi=1/(1+e^{-\eta})ϕ=1/(1+e−η). GLMs set η=θTx\eta=\theta^Txη=θTx; the sigmoid falls out. This is exactly what Lecture 4 does.

3. Two Gaussians with shared covariance give it to you. If x∣y=0x\mid y{=}0x∣y=0 and x∣y=1x\mid y{=}1x∣y=1 are Gaussian with the same covariance matrix, then Bayes' rule makes the posterior p(y=1∣x)p(y{=}1\mid x)p(y=1∣x) exactly a sigmoid of a linear function of xxx. (This is Gaussian Discriminant Analysis, CS229 Lecture 5.)

The probabilistic model

The recipe from topic 2, with Bernoulli in place of Gaussian. Interpret the hypothesis as the probability of the positive class:

P(y=1∣x;θ)=hθ(x),P(y=0∣x;θ)=1−hθ(x)P(y=1\mid x;\theta)=h_\theta(x),\qquad P(y=0\mid x;\theta)=1-h_\theta(x)P(y=1∣x;θ)=hθ​(x),P(y=0∣x;θ)=1−hθ​(x)

The decision boundary is a straight line

Predict y=1y=1y=1 when hθ(x)≥0.5h_\theta(x)\ge0.5hθ​(x)≥0.5. Since g(z)≥12g(z)\ge\tfrac12g(z)≥21​ exactly when z≥0z\ge0z≥0, this is the same as predicting y=1y=1y=1 when θTx≥0\theta^Tx\ge0θTx≥0. So the boundary is the set {x:θTx=0}\{x:\theta^Tx=0\}{x:θTx=0} — a hyperplane. The probabilities curve; the boundary does not.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 11 · Ng asserts "no local optima" — here is the proof

The lecture states that ℓ(θ)\ell(\theta)ℓ(θ) has no local maxima other than the global one and moves on. The proof is short and worth doing, because it is the reason logistic regression is trustworthy in a way that neural networks are not.

Differentiate the gradient once more. From step 6 above, ∂ℓ∂θj=∑i(y(i)−hi)xj(i)\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_i\left(y^{(i)}-h_i\right)x^{(i)}_j∂θj​∂ℓ​=∑i​(y(i)−hi​)xj(i)​, and only hih_ihi​ depends on θ\thetaθ:

∂2ℓ∂θj ∂θk=−∑i=1m∂hi∂θkxj(i)=−∑i=1mhi(1−hi)xk(i)xj(i)\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\theta_j\,\partial\theta_k}=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial\theta_k}x^{(i)}_j=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}h_i\left(1-h_i\right)x^{(i)}_k x^{(i)}_j∂θj​∂θk​∂2ℓ​=−i=1∑m​∂θk​∂hi​​xj(i)​=−i=1∑m​hi​(1−hi​)xk(i)​xj(i)​

In matrix form, with D=diag⁡ ⁣(hi(1−hi))D=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(h_i(1-h_i)\right)D=diag(hi​(1−hi​)):

H=−XTDXH=-X^TDXH=−XTDX

Now take any vector vvv and compute the quadratic form:

vTHv=−vTXTDXv=−(Xv)TD(Xv)=−∑i=1mhi(1−hi)(x(i)Tv)2  ≤  0v^THv=-v^TX^TDXv=-(Xv)^TD(Xv)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}h_i\left(1-h_i\right)\left(x^{(i)T}v\right)^2\;\le\;0vTHv=−vTXTDXv=−(Xv)TD(Xv)=−i=1∑m​hi​(1−hi​)(x(i)Tv)2≤0

Every term is a non-negative weight hi(1−hi)>0h_i(1-h_i)>0hi​(1−hi​)>0 times a square. So HHH is negative semidefinite everywhere, ℓ\ellℓ is concave, and any stationary point is a global maximum. If in addition XXX has full column rank and no hih_ihi​ is exactly 0 or 1, the inequality is strict, ℓ\ellℓ is strictly concave, and the maximiser is unique when it exists.

Gap 12 · "when it exists" is doing real work — separable data has no MLE

Here is a failure the lecture never mentions and that you will hit the first time you run logistic regression on clean data. Suppose some θ\thetaθ separates the classes perfectly: θTx(i)>0\theta^Tx^{(i)}>0θTx(i)>0 for every positive example and <0<0<0 for every negative one. Then scale it up. Replacing θ\thetaθ by cθc\thetacθ for c>1c>1c>1 pushes every hih_ihi​ closer to its correct label, so ℓ(cθ)\ell(c\theta)ℓ(cθ) strictly increases with ccc and approaches its supremum of 000 as c→∞c\to\inftyc→∞ without ever attaining it.

The maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. Gradient ascent will not error out — it will just run forever with ∥θ∥\|\theta\|∥θ∥ growing, printing ever-better training accuracy while producing wildly overconfident probabilities. Newton's method does worse: D→0D\to0D→0, the Hessian becomes singular, and the solve blows up.

The fix is regularisation. Maximise ℓ(θ)−λ2∥θ1:n∥2\ell(\theta)-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta_{1:n}\|^2ℓ(θ)−2λ​∥θ1:n​∥2 instead (leave θ0\theta_0θ0​ unpenalised), which adds −λθj-\lambda\theta_j−λθj​ to the gradient and −λI-\lambda I−λI to the Hessian. The objective becomes strictly concave, the maximiser exists and is unique, and the Hessian is guaranteed invertible. This is why scikit-learn's LogisticRegression is regularised by default — a decision that confuses everyone who learned the unregularised version first.

Gap 13 · four things you need before you ship a logistic regression

Numerical stability. Computing log⁡(1+ez)\log(1+e^{z})log(1+ez) directly overflows for z≳710z\gtrsim 710z≳710 in float64. Use np.logaddexp(0, z) or a softplus that switches to zzz for large zzz; use scipy.special.expit rather than a hand-written sigmoid. And never compute log(h) when h may have rounded to exactly 0.

The 0.5 threshold is a choice, not part of the model. The model outputs a probability; converting it to a decision requires a threshold, and 0.50.50.5 is optimal only when the two kinds of mistake cost the same and the classes are balanced. For a cancer screen, a false negative costs far more than a false positive and the threshold should be far below 0.50.50.5. Evaluate with ROC-AUC or precision–recall, not accuracy, when classes are imbalanced.

Feature scaling. Not required for correctness — the optimum is the same — but wildly-different feature scales make the log-likelihood contours long and thin, and gradient ascent then crawls (this is precisely the shape you will see in Fig. 13). Standardise.

More than two classes. Logistic regression as written handles y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1} only. The generalisation is the softmax (multinomial logistic) model, P(y=k∣x)=eθkTx/∑jeθjTxP(y{=}k\mid x)=e^{\theta_k^Tx}/\sum_j e^{\theta_j^Tx}P(y=k∣x)=eθkT​x/∑j​eθjT​x, which CS229 derives as a GLM in the next lecture. Everything here — concavity, the (y−h)x(y-h)x(y−h)x gradient form, Newton's method — carries over.

04 · Topic 4

Newton's method

Gradient ascent asks "which way is up?". Newton's method asks "where is the top of the parabola that looks like this?" — and jumps straight there.

Start with root-finding

Forget optimisation for a moment. Suppose you have a function fff and you want a θ\thetaθ with f(θ)=0f(\theta)=0f(θ)=0. Newton's idea: replace fff by its tangent line at the current guess, and take the tangent's root as the next guess.

Derivation 5 · the Newton step for a root
  1. The tangent line to fff at the current point θ\thetaθ is   y=f(θ)+f′(θ) (t−θ)\;y=f(\theta)+f'(\theta)\,(t-\theta)y=f(θ)+f′(θ)(t−θ).
  2. Set y=0y=0y=0 and solve for ttt:   0=f(θ)+f′(θ)(t−θ)  ⟹  t−θ=−f(θ)f′(θ)\;0=f(\theta)+f'(\theta)(t-\theta)\;\Longrightarrow\;t-\theta=-\dfrac{f(\theta)}{f'(\theta)}0=f(θ)+f′(θ)(t−θ)⟹t−θ=−f′(θ)f(θ)​.
  3. That ttt is the new iterate.
     θ:=θ−f(θ)f′(θ) \boxed{\ \theta := \theta-\frac{f(\theta)}{f'(\theta)}\ } θ:=θ−f′(θ)f(θ)​ ​
    Geometrically: drop from the curve to the tangent, slide down the tangent to the horizontal axis, and stand there. Ng draws exactly this on the board, and calls the horizontal move Δ\DeltaΔ.

Turn it into a maximiser

We do not want a root of ℓ\ellℓ — we want a maximum. At a maximum the derivative is zero, so apply root-finding to f=ℓ′f=\ell'f=ℓ′:

θ:=θ−ℓ′(θ)ℓ′′(θ)\theta:=\theta-\frac{\ell'(\theta)}{\ell''(\theta)}θ:=θ−ℓ′′(θ)ℓ′(θ)​

and in the general vector case, with ∇θℓ∈Rn+1\nabla_\theta\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}∇θ​ℓ∈Rn+1 the gradient and H∈R(n+1)×(n+1)H\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)}H∈R(n+1)×(n+1) the Hessian, Hjk=∂2ℓ∂θj∂θkH_{jk}=\dfrac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\theta_j\partial\theta_k}Hjk​=∂θj​∂θk​∂2ℓ​:

Newton–Raphson update

θ:=θ−H−1∇θℓ(θ)\theta := \theta - H^{-1}\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta)θ:=θ−H−1∇θ​ℓ(θ)

Trap · that minus sign looks wrong for a maximisation

Every student stumbles here: we are climbing, so why is there a minus? Because HHH is negative definite near a maximum. Writing H=−MH=-MH=−M with MMM positive definite, the update is θ:=θ+M−1∇ℓ\theta:=\theta+M^{-1}\nabla\ellθ:=θ+M−1∇ℓ — a step in a direction that has positive inner product with the gradient, i.e. uphill. The minus sign belongs to the Hessian's sign, not to the direction of travel. The identical formula minimises when HHH is positive definite, which is why the same line of code serves both cases.

Where the formula really comes from

The root-finding story is how Ng motivates it, but the deeper derivation is one line of Taylor expansion, and it generalises better. Expand ℓ\ellℓ to second order around the current θ\thetaθ:

ℓ(θ+Δ)  ≈  ℓ(θ)+∇ℓTΔ+12ΔTHΔ\ell(\theta+\Delta)\;\approx\;\ell(\theta)+\nabla\ell^{T}\Delta+\tfrac12\Delta^{T}H\Deltaℓ(θ+Δ)≈ℓ(θ)+∇ℓTΔ+21​ΔTHΔ

Maximise the right-hand side over Δ\DeltaΔ by setting its gradient to zero: ∇ℓ+HΔ=0\nabla\ell+H\Delta=0∇ℓ+HΔ=0, hence Δ=−H−1∇ℓ\Delta=-H^{-1}\nabla\ellΔ=−H−1∇ℓ. So Newton's method builds a quadratic model of the objective and jumps to that model's peak. Gradient ascent, by contrast, builds a linear model, which has no peak — which is exactly why it needs a step size α\alphaα and Newton does not.

The Hessian for logistic regression

We computed it in Gap 11 while proving concavity. Collected here because you need it to actually run the algorithm:

∇θℓ=XT(y−h),H=−XTDX,D=diag⁡(hi(1−hi))\nabla_\theta\ell = X^T\left(y-h\right),\qquad H=-X^TDX,\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}\Big(h_i\left(1-h_i\right)\Big)∇θ​ℓ=XT(y−h),H=−XTDX,D=diag(hi​(1−hi​))

so the update is

θ:=θ+(XTDX)−1XT(y−h)\theta := \theta + \left(X^TDX\right)^{-1}X^T\left(y-h\right)θ:=θ+(XTDX)−1XT(y−h)

Ng mentions in passing that applying Newton's method to logistic regression is called Fisher scoring. Two things he does not say. First, Fisher scoring in general uses the expected Hessian (the negative Fisher information) rather than the observed one; for a GLM with its canonical link — logistic regression included — the two are equal, so here the distinction collapses and the names are interchangeable. Second, the update has a beautiful alternative reading:

Derivation 6 · Newton's method is iteratively reweighted least squares
  1. Start from the update in the form (XTDX)θnew=(XTDX)θ+XT(y−h)\left(X^TDX\right)\theta_{\text{new}}=\left(X^TDX\right)\theta+X^T(y-h)(XTDX)θnew​=(XTDX)θ+XT(y−h).
  2. Insert DD−1=ID D^{-1}=IDD−1=I into the second term on the right:   XT(y−h)=XTD D−1(y−h)\;X^T(y-h)=X^TD\,D^{-1}(y-h)XT(y−h)=XTDD−1(y−h).
  3. Factor XTDX^TDXTD out of the whole right-hand side.
    (XTDX)θnew=XTD(Xθ+D−1(y−h)⏟z, the “adjusted response”)\left(X^TDX\right)\theta_{\text{new}}=X^TD\Big(\underbrace{X\theta+D^{-1}(y-h)}_{\textstyle z,\ \text{the ``adjusted response''}}\Big)(XTDX)θnew​=XTD(z, the “adjusted response”Xθ+D−1(y−h)​​)
  4. Recognise the shape.
    θnew=(XTDX)−1XTDz\theta_{\text{new}}=\left(X^TDX\right)^{-1}X^TDzθnew​=(XTDX)−1XTDz
    Compare with Derivation 1: this is exactly the weighted normal equation θ=(XTWX)−1XTWy\theta=(X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWyθ=(XTWX)−1XTWy with weights W=DW=DW=D and targets zzz. Every Newton step for logistic regression is a weighted least-squares fit — hence the name IRLS. The weights hi(1−hi)h_i(1-h_i)hi​(1−hi​) are largest for the examples the model is most unsure about, so each step pays most attention to the points near the boundary. This is how R's glm() and most classical GLM software are implemented.

Why it converges so fast

Ng says Newton's method enjoys "quadratic convergence" and that the number of correct digits roughly doubles per iteration. Here is where that comes from.

Derivation 7 · quadratic convergence
  1. Let θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆ be the root of fff and ek=θk−θ⋆e_k=\theta_k-\theta^\starek​=θk​−θ⋆ the error. Taylor-expand fff about θk\theta_kθk​ and evaluate at θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆, with ξ\xiξ between them:
    0=f(θ⋆)=f(θk)+f′(θk)(θ⋆−θk)+12f′′(ξ)(θ⋆−θk)20=f(\theta^\star)=f(\theta_k)+f'(\theta_k)\left(\theta^\star-\theta_k\right)+\tfrac12 f''(\xi)\left(\theta^\star-\theta_k\right)^20=f(θ⋆)=f(θk​)+f′(θk​)(θ⋆−θk​)+21​f′′(ξ)(θ⋆−θk​)2
  2. Divide through by f′(θk)f'(\theta_k)f′(θk​), assumed non-zero:
    0=f(θk)f′(θk)−ek+f′′(ξ)2f′(θk)ek20=\frac{f(\theta_k)}{f'(\theta_k)}-e_k+\frac{f''(\xi)}{2f'(\theta_k)}e_k^{2}0=f′(θk​)f(θk​)​−ek​+2f′(θk​)f′′(ξ)​ek2​
  3. The Newton step is θk+1=θk−f(θk)f′(θk)\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\dfrac{f(\theta_k)}{f'(\theta_k)}θk+1​=θk​−f′(θk​)f(θk​)​, so f(θk)f′(θk)=θk−θk+1=ek−ek+1\dfrac{f(\theta_k)}{f'(\theta_k)}=\theta_k-\theta_{k+1}=e_k-e_{k+1}f′(θk​)f(θk​)​=θk​−θk+1​=ek​−ek+1​. Substitute:
    0=(ek−ek+1)−ek+f′′(ξ)2f′(θk)ek20=\left(e_k-e_{k+1}\right)-e_k+\frac{f''(\xi)}{2f'(\theta_k)}e_k^{2}0=(ek​−ek+1​)−ek​+2f′(θk​)f′′(ξ)​ek2​
  4. Cancel and rearrange:
     ek+1=f′′(ξ)2f′(θk) ek2 \boxed{\ e_{k+1}=\frac{f''(\xi)}{2f'(\theta_k)}\,e_k^{2}\ } ek+1​=2f′(θk​)f′′(ξ)​ek2​ ​
    The new error is proportional to the square of the old one. If ek≈10−3e_k\approx10^{-3}ek​≈10−3, then ek+1≈10−6e_{k+1}\approx10^{-6}ek+1​≈10−6, then 10−1210^{-12}10−12: three iterations to go from three correct digits to twelve. Gradient descent, by contrast, gives ek+1≈c eke_{k+1}\approx c\,e_kek+1​≈cek​ with c<1c<1c<1 — linear convergence, a fixed number of digits per iteration.

The cost, and Ng's rule of thumb

HHH is (n+1)×(n+1)(n{+}1)\times(n{+}1)(n+1)×(n+1). Forming XTDXX^TDXXTDX costs O(mn2)O(mn^2)O(mn2) and solving the system costs O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3). A gradient step costs O(mn)O(mn)O(mn). So Newton's method trades a small number of expensive iterations for a large number of cheap ones, and the exchange rate depends entirely on nnn.

Ng's guidance: use Newton's method when the number of parameters is modest — his figure is roughly 50, "maybe a few hundred". For a problem with tens of thousands of parameters, inverting a Hessian of that size every iteration is out of the question, and you use first-order methods. This is exactly why deep learning uses SGD and Adam rather than Newton's method.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 14 · plain Newton is not globally convergent, and this bites in practice

The lecture presents Newton's method as strictly better than gradient descent apart from cost. It is not. Newton's method is only locally convergent: the quadratic-convergence result in Derivation 7 assumes you are already close enough that the quadratic model is a good approximation. Start too far away and it can oscillate or diverge outright.

This is not hypothetical. On the logistic problem plotted in Fig. 12, starting Newton from θ=(0,0)\theta=(0,0)θ=(0,0) converges in four steps; starting it from a point about two units further out sends ∥θ∥\|\theta\|∥θ∥ to 1020010^{200}10200 within five iterations and then the Hessian solve fails. The mechanism is simple: far from the optimum every hih_ihi​ saturates to 0 or 1, so D→0D\to0D→0, so H→0H\to0H→0, so H−1H^{-1}H−1 explodes.

The fix, which every real implementation uses: take a damped step, θ:=θ+tΔ\theta:=\theta+t\Deltaθ:=θ+tΔ with Δ=−H−1∇ℓ\Delta=-H^{-1}\nabla\ellΔ=−H−1∇ℓ and t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1]t∈(0,1] chosen by backtracking line search — start at t=1t=1t=1, and halve until the objective actually improves. Near the optimum t=1t=1t=1 is accepted immediately and you recover pure Newton with its quadratic rate; far away, the damping keeps you out of trouble. Guaranteed convergence from any start, quadratic convergence at the end.

Gap 15 · four implementation facts

Never form H−1H^{-1}H−1. The formula says H−1∇ℓH^{-1}\nabla\ellH−1∇ℓ; the code should say np.linalg.solve(H, grad). Explicit inversion costs more and is less numerically stable. When HHH is negative definite, a Cholesky factorisation of −H-H−H is faster still.

Guard the Hessian. On separable or near-separable data D→0D\to 0D→0 and HHH becomes singular. Adding the regulariser from Gap 12 contributes −λI-\lambda I−λI to HHH, which bounds its eigenvalues away from zero and fixes both problems at once.

Quasi-Newton is what you will actually use. BFGS and its limited-memory variant L-BFGS build an approximation to H−1H^{-1}H−1 from successive gradients, at O(n)O(n)O(n) memory and no second derivatives. Superlinear rather than quadratic convergence, but no Hessian to form or store — which is why sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression defaults to the lbfgs solver. The lecture never mentions the family.

Newton is affine-invariant. Rescale a feature by a factor of 1000 and gradient descent's behaviour changes completely; Newton's iterates are unchanged. This — not just the iteration count — is the deep reason it needs no learning rate.

A one-line result worth knowing

Run Newton's method on linear regression and it converges in exactly one step, from any starting point, landing on the normal equation. The reason is immediate from the Taylor derivation: J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ) is exactly quadratic in θ\thetaθ, so the second-order model is not an approximation but the function itself, and jumping to the model's optimum jumps to the true optimum. Work through it in problem 5.

The last column is identical in every row. That is not a coincidence and it is not four separate miracles — it is a theorem about generalised linear models: for any exponential-family response with its canonical link, the gradient of the log-likelihood is (y−E[y∣x])x\left(y-\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]\right)x(y−E[y∣x])x. Lecture 4 proves it. Everything in today's lecture is a special case, which is why the LMS-looking update in topic 3 was worth pausing on.

The takeaway to carry into Lecture 4

You are not learning a catalogue of algorithms. You are learning one algorithm — write p(y∣x;θ)p(y\mid x;\theta)p(y∣x;θ), take logs, climb — instantiated at different distributions. Pick the distribution that matches your response variable, and the learning rule writes itself.

07 · Practice

Problems, with full solutions

Ordered from mechanical to genuinely hard. Do them with the solution hidden; every one is the kind of thing CS229 problem sets and midterms actually ask.

P1Derive the closed form for locally weighted regression from scratch.

Solution. This is Derivation 1 above. The two things to be careful about: (i) writing the weighted sum as (y−Xθ)TW(y−Xθ)(y-X\theta)^TW(y-X\theta)(y−Xθ)TW(y−Xθ) requires noticing that WWW diagonal makes the cross terms equal, so they combine into −2θTXTWy-2\theta^TX^TWy−2θTXTWy; (ii) the stationary point is a minimum because ∇2JW=2XTWX\nabla^2 J_W=2X^TWX∇2JW​=2XTWX is positive semidefinite whenever every w(i)≥0w^{(i)}\ge0w(i)≥0 — which holds since each weight is an exponential. Answer: θ=(XTWX)−1XTWy\theta=(X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWyθ=(XTWX)−1XTWy.

P2Show that locally weighted regression degenerates to ordinary linear regression as τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞. What happens as τ→0+\tau\to0^+τ→0+?

As τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞: for any fixed pair x(i),xx^{(i)},xx(i),x, the exponent −(x(i)−x)2/(2τ2)→0-\left(x^{(i)}-x\right)^2/(2\tau^2)\to0−(x(i)−x)2/(2τ2)→0, so w(i)→e0=1w^{(i)}\to e^0=1w(i)→e0=1 for every iii. Then W→IW\to IW→I and the estimator becomes (XTX)−1XTy(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty(XTX)−1XTy — ordinary least squares, the same θ\thetaθ for every query. The middle panel of Fig. 3 with τ=1.6\tau=1.6τ=1.6 is already visibly heading toward the straight line in the first panel.

As τ→0+\tau\to0^+τ→0+: all weights except those of the very nearest points underflow to zero. Two things go wrong. Statistically, the fit is determined by a handful of points, so variance explodes and the curve becomes jagged (Fig. 3, τ=0.08\tau=0.08τ=0.08). Numerically, XTWXX^TWXXTWX becomes singular once fewer than n+1n{+}1n+1 points have non-negligible weight, and the solve fails — which is why the code in topic 1 adds a small ridge term.

P3Prove g′(z)=g(z)(1−g(z))g'(z)=g(z)\left(1-g(z)\right)g′(z)=g(z)(1−g(z)), then use it to show ∂∂θjhθ(x)=hθ(x)(1−hθ(x))xj\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}h_\theta(x)=h_\theta(x)\left(1-h_\theta(x)\right)x_j∂θj​∂​hθ​(x)=hθ​(x)(1−hθ​(x))xj​.

Solution. The first part is the Lemma in topic 3 — chain rule on (1+e−z)−1(1+e^{-z})^{-1}(1+e−z)−1, then split the fraction and use e−z=(1+e−z)−1e^{-z}=(1+e^{-z})-1e−z=(1+e−z)−1.

For the second part, hθ(x)=g(θTx)h_\theta(x)=g(\theta^Tx)hθ​(x)=g(θTx), so by the chain rule ∂∂θjhθ(x)=g′(θTx)⋅∂∂θj(θTx)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}h_\theta(x)=g'(\theta^Tx)\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\left(\theta^Tx\right)∂θj​∂​hθ​(x)=g′(θTx)⋅∂θj​∂​(θTx). The inner derivative is xjx_jxj​, because θTx=∑kθkxk\theta^Tx=\sum_k\theta_kx_kθTx=∑k​θk​xk​ and only the k=jk=jk=j term survives. Substituting the identity gives hθ(x)(1−hθ(x))xjh_\theta(x)\left(1-h_\theta(x)\right)x_jhθ​(x)(1−hθ​(x))xj​.

P4Prove that the logistic log-likelihood is concave, and state precisely when it is strictly concave.

Solution. Compute H=−XTDXH=-X^TDXH=−XTDX with D=diag⁡(hi(1−hi))D=\operatorname{diag}(h_i(1-h_i))D=diag(hi​(1−hi​)) as in Gap 11, then for arbitrary v∈Rn+1v\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}v∈Rn+1:

vTHv=−(Xv)TD(Xv)=−∑i=1mhi(1−hi)(x(i)Tv)2≤0.v^THv=-(Xv)^TD(Xv)=-\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(1-h_i)\left(x^{(i)T}v\right)^2\le 0.vTHv=−(Xv)TD(Xv)=−i=1∑m​hi​(1−hi​)(x(i)Tv)2≤0.

So H⪯0H\preceq0H⪯0 everywhere and ℓ\ellℓ is concave; every stationary point is therefore a global maximum, and there are no local maxima to get stuck in.

Strictness. The sum is zero only if every term is zero. Since 0<hi<10<h_i<10<hi​<1 always (the sigmoid never attains its asymptotes for finite θTx\theta^TxθTx), each coefficient hi(1−hi)h_i(1-h_i)hi​(1−hi​) is strictly positive, so the sum vanishes only when x(i)Tv=0x^{(i)T}v=0x(i)Tv=0 for all iii — that is, when Xv=0Xv=0Xv=0. Hence ℓ\ellℓ is strictly concave iff XXX has full column rank (no exactly redundant features, and m≥n+1m\ge n+1m≥n+1). Note that strict concavity gives uniqueness if a maximiser exists, which P7 shows can fail.

P5Show that Newton's method applied to linear regression converges in exactly one iteration, from any starting point, and that the answer is the normal equation.

Solution. Write J(θ)=12∥Xθ−y∥2J(\theta)=\frac12\|X\theta-y\|^2J(θ)=21​∥Xθ−y∥2. Then

∇J=XT(Xθ−y),H=∇2J=XTX,\nabla J=X^T(X\theta-y),\qquad H=\nabla^2 J=X^TX,∇J=XT(Xθ−y),H=∇2J=XTX,

and the Hessian does not depend on θ\thetaθ at all. One Newton step from any θ(0)\theta^{(0)}θ(0):

θ(1)=θ(0)−(XTX)−1XT(Xθ(0)−y)=θ(0)−(XTX)−1(XTX)⏟= Iθ(0)+(XTX)−1XTy\theta^{(1)}=\theta^{(0)}-\left(X^TX\right)^{-1}X^T\left(X\theta^{(0)}-y\right)=\theta^{(0)}-\underbrace{\left(X^TX\right)^{-1}\left(X^TX\right)}_{=\,I}\theta^{(0)}+\left(X^TX\right)^{-1}X^Tyθ(1)=θ(0)−(XTX)−1XT(Xθ(0)−y)=θ(0)−=I(XTX)−1(XTX)​​θ(0)+(XTX)−1XTy

=(XTX)−1XTy.=\left(X^TX\right)^{-1}X^Ty.=(XTX)−1XTy.

Why, conceptually. Newton's method maximises a second-order Taylor model of the objective. For a quadratic objective that model is exact, not an approximation — so jumping to the model's optimum lands on the true optimum. This also explains why the normal equation and Newton's method give the same formula: they are the same computation.

P6Place a prior θ∼N(0,τ2I)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2I)θ∼N(0,τ2I) on the parameters of linear regression and find the MAP estimate. Identify the result.

Solution. MAP maximises the posterior, which by Bayes' rule is proportional to prior times likelihood:

θ^MAP=arg⁡max⁡θ log⁡p(θ)+∑i=1mlog⁡p ⁣(y(i)∣x(i),θ).\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_\theta\ \log p(\theta)+\sum_{i=1}^m\log p\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)},\theta\right).θ^MAP​=argθmax​ logp(θ)+i=1∑m​logp(y(i)∣x(i),θ).

The prior contributes log⁡p(θ)=−12τ2∥θ∥2+const\log p(\theta)=-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\theta\|^2+\text{const}logp(θ)=−2τ21​∥θ∥2+const; the likelihood contributes −12σ2∑i(y(i)−θTx(i))2+const-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2+\text{const}−2σ21​∑i​(y(i)−θTx(i))2+const from Derivation 2. Flipping the sign to a minimisation and multiplying through by σ2\sigma^2σ2:

θ^MAP=arg⁡min⁡θ 12∑i=1m(y(i)−θTx(i))2+λ2∥θ∥2,λ=σ2τ2.\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\min_\theta\ \frac12\sum_{i=1}^m\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^2,\qquad \lambda=\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.θ^MAP​=argθmin​ 21​i=1∑m​(y(i)−θTx(i))2+2λ​∥θ∥2,λ=τ2σ2​.

This is ridge regression, with closed form θ=(XTX+λI)−1XTy\theta=(X^TX+\lambda I)^{-1}X^Tyθ=(XTX+λI)−1XTy. Read the ratio: a tight prior (small τ\tauτ) or noisy data (large σ\sigmaσ) both push λ\lambdaλ up and shrink θ\thetaθ toward zero. Replacing the Gaussian prior with a Laplace prior p(θj)∝e−∣θj∣/bp(\theta_j)\propto e^{-|\theta_j|/b}p(θj​)∝e−∣θj​∣/b gives an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty — the LASSO.

P7Prove that if the training data are linearly separable, the logistic-regression MLE does not exist.

Solution. Suppose θ0\theta_0θ0​ separates the classes strictly: θ0Tx(i)>0\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}>0θ0T​x(i)>0 whenever y(i)=1y^{(i)}=1y(i)=1 and θ0Tx(i)<0\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}<0θ0T​x(i)<0 whenever y(i)=0y^{(i)}=0y(i)=0. Consider the scaled family θ=c θ0\theta=c\,\theta_0θ=cθ0​ for c>0c>0c>0 and evaluate the log-likelihood term by term.

For a positive example, the contribution is log⁡h=log⁡g ⁣(c θ0Tx(i))\log h=\log g\!\left(c\,\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}\right)logh=logg(cθ0T​x(i)). Since θ0Tx(i)>0\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}>0θ0T​x(i)>0, increasing ccc increases the argument, and ggg is strictly increasing, so log⁡h\log hlogh strictly increases toward log⁡1=0\log 1=0log1=0. For a negative example the contribution is log⁡(1−h)=log⁡g ⁣(−c θ0Tx(i))\log(1-h)=\log g\!\left(-c\,\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}\right)log(1−h)=logg(−cθ0T​x(i)), and since −θ0Tx(i)>0-\theta_0^Tx^{(i)}>0−θ0T​x(i)>0 the same argument applies.

Therefore ℓ(cθ0)\ell(c\theta_0)ℓ(cθ0​) is strictly increasing in ccc with lim⁡c→∞ℓ(cθ0)=0\lim_{c\to\infty}\ell(c\theta_0)=0limc→∞​ℓ(cθ0​)=0, and ℓ<0\ell<0ℓ<0 everywhere. The supremum 000 is approached but never attained, so no maximiser exists and ∥θ^∥=∞\|\hat\theta\|=\infty∥θ^∥=∞.

Consequence. Gradient ascent diverges slowly (Fig. 11, middle) and Newton's method fails hard, because D→0D\to0D→0 makes HHH singular. Adding −λ2∥θ∥2-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^2−2λ​∥θ∥2 makes the objective strictly concave and coercive (ℓλ→−∞\ell_\lambda\to-\inftyℓλ​→−∞ as ∥θ∥→∞\|\theta\|\to\infty∥θ∥→∞), which restores existence and uniqueness.

P8Suppose the noise variance differs per example: ε(i)∼N(0,σi2)\varepsilon^{(i)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_i^2)ε(i)∼N(0,σi2​) with known σi\sigma_iσi​. Derive the MLE and compare it to topic 1.

Solution. Redo Derivation 2 keeping σi\sigma_iσi​ inside the sum. Step 5 becomes

ℓ(θ)=∑i=1m[−log⁡(2π σi)−(y(i)−θTx(i))22σi2],\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^m\left[-\log\left(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_i\right)-\frac{\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\right],ℓ(θ)=i=1∑m​[−log(2π​σi​)−2σi2​(y(i)−θTx(i))2​],

and the σi\sigma_iσi​ can no longer be pulled out. Dropping the θ\thetaθ-independent first term, maximising ℓ\ellℓ means

min⁡θ ∑i=1m1σi2(y(i)−θTx(i))2,\min_\theta\ \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}\left(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)}\right)^2,θmin​ i=1∑m​σi2​1​(y(i)−θTx(i))2,

which is weighted least squares with w(i)=1/σi2w^{(i)}=1/\sigma_i^2w(i)=1/σi2​, solved by θ=(XTWX)−1XTWy\theta=(X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWyθ=(XTWX)−1XTWy — the identical formula you derived for locally weighted regression.

The point of the problem. Same algebra, entirely different meaning. In LWR the weights encode proximity to the query point and change with every prediction. Here they encode measurement precision and are a fixed property of the data: noisy observations get listened to less. Recognising a shared computational skeleton under different modelling stories is most of what mathematical maturity in this course consists of.

P9Show that squared loss applied to the sigmoid output is not convex in θ\thetaθ — with an explicit second derivative.

Solution. Take the simplest possible case: one feature x=1x=1x=1, one example with label y=1y=1y=1, so L(θ)=(g(θ)−1)2=(1−g)2L(\theta)=\left(g(\theta)-1\right)^2=\left(1-g\right)^2L(θ)=(g(θ)−1)2=(1−g)2 where g=g(θ)g=g(\theta)g=g(θ).

First derivative, using g′=g(1−g)g'=g(1-g)g′=g(1−g):

L′(θ)=2(1−g)⋅(−g′)=−2g(1−g)2.L'(\theta)=2\left(1-g\right)\cdot\left(-g'\right)=-2g\left(1-g\right)^2.L′(θ)=2(1−g)⋅(−g′)=−2g(1−g)2.

Second derivative, product rule:

L′′(θ)=−2[g′(1−g)2+g⋅2(1−g)(−g′)]=−2g′(1−g)[(1−g)−2g]=−2g(1−g)2(1−3g).L''(\theta)=-2\Big[g'\left(1-g\right)^2+g\cdot2\left(1-g\right)\left(-g'\right)\Big]=-2g'\left(1-g\right)\Big[\left(1-g\right)-2g\Big]=-2g\left(1-g\right)^2\left(1-3g\right).L′′(θ)=−2[g′(1−g)2+g⋅2(1−g)(−g′)]=−2g′(1−g)[(1−g)−2g]=−2g(1−g)2(1−3g).

The factor −2g(1−g)2-2g(1-g)^2−2g(1−g)2 is strictly negative, so the sign of L′′L''L′′ is the sign of −(1−3g)-(1-3g)−(1−3g), i.e. L′′<0L''<0L′′<0 whenever g<13g<\tfrac13g<31​. The loss is concave in that whole region, so it is not convex, and gradient descent can stall on a plateau far from the answer.

Two takeaways. Analytically, this is why the course does not simply reuse squared error for classification. Practically, notice from the formula that L′→0L'\to0L′→0 as g→0g\to0g→0: a maximally wrong prediction produces a vanishing gradient. Log loss has ∂ℓ/∂θ=(y−g)x\partial\ell/\partial\theta=(y-g)x∂ℓ/∂θ=(y−g)x, which stays at magnitude 1 in exactly that regime — the wrongest predictions push hardest. That is the right-hand panel of Fig. 9.

P10Harder. Show that locally weighted regression is a linear smoother: its fitted values are a fixed matrix times yyy. Why does this let you count the model's effective number of parameters?

Solution. Fix a query point xxx. The weights w(i)w^{(i)}w(i) depend on the inputs and on xxx, but not on yyy at all. So the prediction is

y^(x)=xT(XTWxX)−1XTWx y  =  ℓ(x)Ty,ℓ(x)T:=xT(XTWxX)−1XTWx,\hat y(x)=x^T\left(X^TW_xX\right)^{-1}X^TW_x\,y \;=\; \ell(x)^T y,\qquad \ell(x)^T := x^T\left(X^TW_xX\right)^{-1}X^TW_x,y^​(x)=xT(XTWx​X)−1XTWx​y=ℓ(x)Ty,ℓ(x)T:=xT(XTWx​X)−1XTWx​,

a fixed vector of coefficients dotted with the response — i.e. the fit is linear in yyy even though it is a nonlinear function of xxx. Stacking the rows ℓ(x(i))T\ell(x^{(i)})^Tℓ(x(i))T for each training point gives y^=Ly\hat y = L yy^​=Ly with L∈Rm×mL\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}L∈Rm×m, the smoother matrix.

Why this is useful. For ordinary linear regression the analogous matrix is the hat matrix H=X(XTX)−1XTH=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^TH=X(XTX)−1XT, and tr⁡(H)=n+1\operatorname{tr}(H)=n+1tr(H)=n+1 — exactly the number of parameters. Defining the effective degrees of freedom of a smoother as tr⁡(L)\operatorname{tr}(L)tr(L) therefore extends the notion of "model size" to a method that has no fixed parameter count. As τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞, tr⁡(L)→n+1\operatorname{tr}(L)\to n+1tr(L)→n+1; as τ→0\tau\to0τ→0, L→IL\to IL→I and tr⁡(L)→m\operatorname{tr}(L)\to mtr(L)→m — one effective parameter per data point, which is a precise statement of what maximal overfitting means. This also makes model-selection criteria such as AIC and generalised cross-validation applicable to locally weighted regression.

08 · Prep

Exam and interview questions

Short answers, phrased the way an examiner or interviewer wants to hear them. Cover the answer and say it out loud before reading.

Conceptual (CS229 midterm style)

Is locally weighted regression parametric or non-parametric, and what exactly makes it so?

Non-parametric — not because it lacks parameters, but because you must retain the entire training set to make a prediction. The amount of information you carry forward grows with mmm rather than being summarised into a fixed-size θ\thetaθ.

What assumptions make least squares the maximum-likelihood estimate?

y(i)=θTx(i)+ε(i)y^{(i)}=\theta^Tx^{(i)}+\varepsilon^{(i)}y(i)=θTx(i)+ε(i) with the ε(i)\varepsilon^{(i)}ε(i) independent and identically distributed N(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2). Independence lets the likelihood factor; the Gaussian's exponent supplies the square; the constant variance lets σ2\sigma^2σ2 factor out.

Why does σ2\sigma^2σ2 not appear in the final answer?

It multiplies the entire θ\thetaθ-dependent term by a positive constant, and a positive constant cannot change where a function is maximised. It reappears the moment you want σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2 itself, prediction intervals, or standard errors.

Logistic regression's update rule looks identical to the LMS rule. Are they the same algorithm?

No — hθh_\thetahθ​ is a different function (g(θTx)g(\theta^Tx)g(θTx) rather than θTx\theta^TxθTx), so the updates compute different numbers. They look alike because both are generalised linear models with their canonical link, where the gradient is always (y−E[y∣x])x\left(y-\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]\right)x(y−E[y∣x])x.

Is the logistic regression decision boundary linear or nonlinear?

Linear in the features you supply. h≥12  ⟺  θTx≥0h\ge\tfrac12 \iff \theta^Tx\ge0h≥21​⟺θTx≥0, a hyperplane. The probability surface is nonlinear; the boundary is not. Curved boundaries require nonlinear features.

Why is the logistic likelihood guaranteed free of local optima?

Its Hessian −XTDX-X^TDX−XTDX satisfies vTHv=−∑ihi(1−hi)(x(i)Tv)2≤0v^THv=-\sum_i h_i(1-h_i)\left(x^{(i)T}v\right)^2\le0vTHv=−∑i​hi​(1−hi​)(x(i)Tv)2≤0 for every vvv, so the log-likelihood is concave and every stationary point is global.

When would you choose Newton's method over gradient descent, and when not?

Choose it when the parameter count is small — roughly up to fifty, maybe a few hundred: it converges quadratically, needs no learning rate, and is affine-invariant. Avoid it when nnn is large (forming and factorising HHH costs O(mn2+n3)O(mn^2+n^3)O(mn2+n3) per step), when the Hessian is singular or indefinite, or when the starting point may be far from the optimum without damping.

What does "quadratic convergence" actually mean?

The error at each step is proportional to the square of the previous error, ek+1=Cek2e_{k+1}=Ce_k^2ek+1​=Cek2​, so the number of correct decimal digits roughly doubles per iteration. Gradient descent is linear: ek+1=ceke_{k+1}=ce_kek+1​=cek​, a fixed number of digits per iteration.

Applied (interview style)

Your logistic regression's coefficients keep growing and training accuracy hits 100%. What is happening?

The data are linearly separable, so the unregularised MLE does not exist and ∥θ∥→∞\|\theta\|\to\infty∥θ∥→∞. Add ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ regularisation, or check for a leaked feature that encodes the label. Probabilities from such a model are meaningless — they will all be near 0 or 1.

Why is scikit-learn's LogisticRegression regularised by default? Isn't that a strange default?

It is a deliberate guard against exactly the failure above, plus multicollinearity. Separability is common in high dimensions and with one-hot features, and an unregularised default would silently produce divergent, overconfident models. Set C large to approach the unregularised fit.

You are asked to interpret a logistic regression coefficient. What do you say?

θj\theta_jθj​ is the change in the log-odds of the positive class per unit increase in xjx_jxj​, holding other features fixed. Exponentiating, eθje^{\theta_j}eθj​ is the multiplicative change in the odds — the odds ratio. It is not a change in probability, because the probability change depends on where on the sigmoid you sit.

Would you use locally weighted regression in a production recommender with 200 features?

No, twice over. The curse of dimensionality means no training point is genuinely "near" a query in 200 dimensions, so the local fit is not local. And every prediction would touch the whole training set at serving time. LWR belongs to low-dimensional problems with abundant data.

Your loss is NaN after a few iterations. Where do you look first?

Overflow in exp⁡\expexp or log⁡(0)\log(0)log(0). Use logaddexp/softplus for log⁡(1+ez)\log(1+e^z)log(1+ez) and a numerically stable sigmoid; clip probabilities away from exactly 0 and 1; check that the learning rate is not so large that θ\thetaθ explodes; and confirm you are not dividing by a DDD that has underflowed in a Newton step.

How do you pick the bandwidth τ\tauτ?

Hold-out or k-fold cross-validation over a log-spaced grid, minimising held-out error. Never training error — it decreases monotonically as τ→0\tau\to0τ→0 and would always select the most overfit model.

What is IRLS?

Iteratively reweighted least squares: the observation that each Newton step for logistic regression is algebraically a weighted least-squares fit, with weights hi(1−hi)h_i(1-h_i)hi​(1−hi​) and an adjusted response z=Xθ+D−1(y−h)z=X\theta+D^{-1}(y-h)z=Xθ+D−1(y−h). It is how classical GLM software is implemented.

09 · Errata for your notes

Nine things students get wrong

Collected from the places this lecture's material reliably goes sideways.

The misconceptionWhat is actually true
"Non-parametric means no parameters."It means no fixed, finite parameter vector that summarises the data. LWR fits a fresh θ\thetaθ per query and keeps every training point.
"The τ\tauτ in the weights is a standard deviation."The weight function is not a probability density — no normalising constant, nothing integrates to 1. It borrows the Gaussian's shape only. Unrelated to the σ\sigmaσ in topic 2.
"Logistic regression is a regression algorithm."It is a classification algorithm. The name is historical: it regresses the log-odds linearly on xxx.
"The sigmoid was chosen arbitrarily among squashing functions."It is the inverse of the logit, the canonical link of the Bernoulli, and the exact posterior form under shared-covariance Gaussian classes. Three independent derivations pick it out (Gap 10).
"Concave log-likelihood means gradient ascent always converges."Concavity rules out local optima; it does not guarantee a maximiser exists. On separable data the supremum is not attained and ∥θ∥\|\theta\|∥θ∥ diverges (Gap 12).
"Newton's method is strictly better than gradient descent, just slower per step."It is only locally convergent. From a far start it can diverge outright — verified on the very dataset in Fig. 12. Real implementations damp it with a line search (Gap 14).
"The minus sign in θ:=θ−H−1∇ℓ\theta:=\theta-H^{-1}\nabla\ellθ:=θ−H−1∇ℓ means we are descending."The sign belongs to the Hessian: HHH is negative definite at a maximum, so −H−1∇ℓ-H^{-1}\nabla\ell−H−1∇ℓ points uphill. The same formula minimises when HHH is positive definite.
"Squared error works fine for classification, it is just less principled."It is non-convex in θ\thetaθ once composed with the sigmoid (L′′<0L''<0L′′<0 for g<13g<\tfrac13g<31​, problem P9), and its gradient vanishes on the most badly wrong predictions.
"p(y∣x,θ)p(y\mid x,\theta)p(y∣x,θ) and p(y∣x;θ)p(y\mid x;\theta)p(y∣x;θ) are the same thing."The comma conditions on θ\thetaθ as a random variable — that is the Bayesian setup that leads to MAP and ridge. The semicolon treats θ\thetaθ as a fixed unknown parameter, which is what "maximum likelihood" presumes.
10 · Where to go next

Sources and further reading

Primary

  • Lecture 3 — Locally Weighted & Logistic Regression, Stanford CS229, Autumn 2018, Andrew Ng. The lecture this guide reconstructs.
  • CS229 main lecture notes (Ng & Ma). Locally weighted regression and the probabilistic interpretation are in §1; classification, logistic regression and Newton's method in §2. The canonical written source for everything above.
  • The full CS229 Autumn 2018 playlist. Lecture 4 (GLMs and the exponential family) is the direct sequel and closes topic 3's open promise.

For the gaps

  • Bias–variance, cross-validation, LOESS, smoother matrices — Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, ch. 6 (kernel smoothing) and ch. 7 (model assessment). Free from the authors' Stanford page.
  • Separability, regularisation, IRLS, GLM theory — ESL §4.4, and McCullagh & Nelder, Generalized Linear Models, for the classical treatment where IRLS is the definition rather than an observation.
  • Newton's method, damping, line search, quasi-Newton — Boyd & Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, ch. 9. Free PDF from Stanford. §9.5 is the definitive treatment of damped Newton and why pure Newton is not enough.
  • MAP, priors, ridge and LASSO as Bayesian estimators — Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction, ch. 11.
